summary: Martian Map is a layered, hyperlocal map and route planner for a human Marswalk. A 3D globe built from NASA/USGS elevation data lets the user pick a mission site and opens a detailed map of the excursion area. We built two sites: Jezero Crater with full routing, and Mount Sharp in Gale Crater with map layers. From NASA Mars Trek data (a 20 m elevation model and aqueous-mineral detections) we compute slopes and mark anything steeper than 25 degrees, a team-chosen limit, as no-go. The user places stops, and an A* algorithm finds the cheapest safe path from the habitat through every stop and back, showing distance, walking time, time at stops and maximum slope against a 6-hour limit. This turns scattered orbital datasets into one usable plan for a single outing, so astronauts and mission planners can see where to go, how long it takes, and that the return is guaranteed. Speed and time limits are our assumptions. Backend code was written with AI assistance (Claude).
details: Martian Map plans a safe, time-limited walk on Mars. A 3D globe built from NASA/USGS elevation data lets the user pick a mission site. A detailed map of the excursion area then opens with toggleable layers: MRO CTX orbital imagery (6 m/pixel), MOLA colour relief, aqueous-mineral detections and a slope hazard map. We compute slopes from the 20 m CTX elevation model of Jezero Crater and turn them into a walking-cost map. Slopes over 25° and a 156 m buffer around them are forbidden. The user clicks stops on the map, and an A* search finds the cheapest safe path from the habitat through every stop and back to the base. The panel shows distance, walking time, time at stops, maximum slope, an elevation profile and a bar comparing the whole excursion with a 6-hour limit. A “walk” mode replays the excursion with a countdown, checkpoints at each stop and alerts when the crew cannot make it back in time. Mission planners, astronauts and scientists get one place where scattered orbital datasets become a concrete plan for a single outing. The safety limits and a guaranteed return are built into the route, not checked afterwards. Python, FastAPI, NumPy and tifffile for the backend and data processing; JavaScript, Three.js (globe) and Leaflet (map) for the frontend; GeoJSON for layers. Data: NASA/JPL Mars Trek (CTX DEM and mosaic, MOLA, aqueous-mineral layer) and USGS Astrogeology products. We connect global and local scales in one flow: globe → site → route. The planner also searches for the cheapest order of stops using true slope-aware path costs, which in our tests shortened random 7-stop routes by up to 43% compared with the clicked order. Cell slope uses the steepest pixel, not the average, to stay conservative. East–west pixel size is corrected for latitude. Speed (2.5 km/h), the 25° limit and the 6-hour limit are our own stated assumptions. Resolution is too coarse to show boulders, and Mount Sharp currently has map layers but no real routing data. We deliberately used only NASA-provided data.
